ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — History and Physical — Ernest Shackleton — True-date frame: synthetic events are moved into the patient's historical lifetime. Codes, instruments, and treatments remain modern and are anachronistic.

code.originalText: New patient visit for chest tightness and breathlessness on exertion in a heavy smoker planning a polar expedition: risk assessment, ECG and blood tests, starting treatment, smoking and alcohol counseling, and a cardiology referral

text.paragraph: New patient visit for chest tightness and breathlessness on exertion in a heavy smoker planning a polar expedition: risk assessment, ECG and blood tests, starting treatment, smoking and alcohol counseling, and a cardiology referral [S]
This fictional modern episode addresses the presenting concerns below. [S]

list.item: He is afraid a heart diagnosis will stop the expedition he has promised to lead. [S]
He will be weeks from a hospital at sea and in the far south. [S]

text.paragraph: Historical basis. These claims are historical evidence, not findings from a modern examination.

list.item: Ernest Henry Shackleton was born on February 15, 1874, at Kilkea, County Kildare, Ireland, the son of Dr. Henry Shackleton, of a well-known Quaker family. [D]

On the southern sledge journey of the Discovery expedition he became unable to pull the sledge because of breathlessness and weakness; the collapse was attributed to scurvy and "a sort of asthma," and he was invalided home against his will in 1903. [D]

On the Nimrod expedition (1907 to 1909), its medical officer Eric Marshall recorded in his diary on January 20, 1908, that Shackleton was very unwell after pulling on a rope, and twice heard a pulmonary systolic murmur. [D]

On the Imperial Trans-Antarctic (Endurance) expedition of 1914 to 1917, of fifty-six men three died in the Antarctic: Mackintosh, Hayward, and Spencer-Smith of the Ross Sea party. No member of the Endurance's own party died. [D]
His colleague Dr. James McIlroy later recalled that on one occasion Shackleton would not undress and let him listen to his heart. [D]
He was a heavy cigarette smoker for most of his life. [D]

After the war he returned to London. In 1921, with John Quiller Rowett taking on practically the whole financial responsibility, he turned his planned Arctic expedition into the Shackleton-Rowett expedition to the South; it was organized and equipped within three months, its sailing was postponed beyond August 20 by a strike of ships' joiners and other delays, and the Quest left St. Katharine's Dock in London on September 17, 1921. [D]

text.paragraph: 5 later historical claims are omitted because they describe events after the index age. See the teaching note.
Historical biography with true dates. These events are not part of the synthetic care timeline.

list.item: Polar explorer and expedition leader; organizing a ship-based scientific expedition to the Antarctic and sub-Antarctic islands that sails from London in about four months, with a long sea passage and weeks out of reach of a hospital [S]
Married; lives in London while he organizes the expedition, working long days on finance, the ship, stores, and the crew [S]
Tobacco: about 25 cigarettes a day since 16 (about 39 pack-years); has never tried to stop; first cigarette within 30 minutes of waking [S]
Alcohol: three or four drinks on most evenings at dinners with backers, more at weekends (AUDIT 12, hazardous range); no withdrawal symptoms; no other drugs [S]
Exercise: none regular since his last expedition; heavy lifting of stores at the dock; walks fast [S]
Does not want anything recorded or done that could stop the expedition; uneasy about being examined, and agreed after his reasons were heard [S]

Cardiology consultation in two weeks with coronary CT angiography for suspected stable angina, and advice on revascularization and on fitness for the expedition. Guideline: 2023 AHA/ACC/ACCP/ASPC/NLA/PCNA Guideline for the Management of Patients With Chronic Coronary Disease (Virani SS, et al. Circulation 2023;148(9):e9-e119) (2023); 2024 ESC Guidelines for the management of chronic coronary syndromes (Vrints C, et al. Eur Heart J 2024;45(36):3415-3537) (2024) [S]

Medical therapy from intake for suspected angina: aspirin 81 mg, atorvastatin 80 mg, metoprolol succinate, and sublingual nitroglycerin with written instructions to call emergency services if pain lasts more than 5 minutes after the first dose. Guideline: 2023 AHA/ACC/ACCP/ASPC/NLA/PCNA Guideline for the Management of Patients With Chronic Coronary Disease (Virani SS, et al. Circulation 2023;148(9):e9-e119) (2023); 2024 ESC Guidelines for the management of chronic coronary syndromes (Vrints C, et al. Eur Heart J 2024;45(36):3415-3537) (2024); CMID: Clinical Monitoring Intelligence Database, ischemic heart disease and hyperlipidemia monographs (2026) [S]

Stop smoking: varenicline for 12 weeks, with the option of 12 more, a quit date in one week, counseling at each visit, and the quitline. Guideline: 2023 AHA/ACC/ACCP/ASPC/NLA/PCNA Guideline for the Management of Patients With Chronic Coronary Disease (Virani SS, et al. Circulation 2023;148(9):e9-e119) (2023); Tobacco Smoking Cessation in Adults, Including Pregnant Persons: Interventions (2021) [S]

AUDIT with a brief intervention for hazardous drinking: no more than two drinks a day and several alcohol-free days a week, with AUDIT-C at follow-up. Guideline: 2023 AHA/ACC/ACCP/ASPC/NLA/PCNA Guideline for the Management of Patients With Chronic Coronary Disease (Virani SS, et al. Circulation 2023;148(9):e9-e119) (2023); Unhealthy Alcohol Use in Adolescents and Adults: Screening and Behavioral Counseling Interventions (2018) [S]

Prediabetes: diet and activity counseling and HbA1c in about four months. Guideline: 2023 AHA/ACC/ACCP/ASPC/NLA/PCNA Guideline for the Management of Patients With Chronic Coronary Disease (Virani SS, et al. Circulation 2023;148(9):e9-e119) (2023); Prediabetes and Type 2 Diabetes: Screening (2021) [S]
